I got this to compare it with the upgraded Greatone emergency radio.  The two models are similar, with the main difference being that this version has fewer features.  This is somewhat more compact than the upgraded model but still has good features.  I couldn't get good reception on it from one of the strongest AM stations in my area.  FM seemed to come in much clearer.  I found one clear WB (weather band) station.  I wouldn't expect top quality sound, as the radio is quite small and compact.  As an emergency radio, this is excellent.  You can charge it with a manual crank, although it takes a LOT of cranking (no different than most radios that charge this way); a solar panel (which I haven't tried yet) or you can charge it from a USB connection. The USB cable is included for that.  If the internal lithium ION rechargeable battery should happen to become discharged before you can get it charged again, you are out of luck, until you can recharge it one of the 3 ways available.  The upgraded version has conventional battery backup, which is better.  On this version, if the rechargeable battery ever dies completely, there is a door with a screw that you can remove to access and replace the battery.  (It should last a very long time and not need replacement.)  Other features:  has an external charging port for a USB device (such as your cellphone) and a light on the end, controlled with a push button switch.  The on/off, volume knob turned easily, but the tuning knob was a little hard to turn.  If conventional battery backup is not important to you, this radio compares favorably to the upgraded version.

I use the sleep headphones because I listen to books to get to sleep. I need the volume quite high because I use hearing aids. This headset is adequate for my purpose. It’s very comfortable to wear, but the controls are not very sensitive.

This AMAZONBASICS FM DUAL ALARM DIGITAL CLOCK RADIO (with USB Charging Port, LED Display) plays FM radio stations only. (It’s not a good choice for a news junkie like myself, as my favorite local news-only stations are all on AM channels.)

The FM radio speaker sounds very tinny, so you won’t want to use the radio to listen to music. It’s okay, I think, for playing FM music to wake you up. If you don’t like the speaker, you can just use the plain alarm-sound option. You can also connect the clock to an auxiliary MP3 device.

The beeper alarm doesn’t sound overly loud to me, even at the maximum volume. It takes many seconds for the volume to increase from the initial faint beep to the maximum. To wake out of a really sound sleep, you need a high-volume alarm.

It’s nice being able to set two different alarms. The alarms are NOT tied to specific days of the week--you just turn on the one you want. One alarm is at the left of the clock, the other is at the right. Two people who rise at different times will like this feature, or one person can use it for something like weekdays and weekends.

The digital display is large enough to read from across a room. However, the display is NOT so bright that it will interfere with sleeping. The time is easy to program by sliding the “Lock” button, holding down the volume button until the correct time is displayed, and sliding the Lock button back to locked position.

Another nice feature is the battery backup. It takes two AAA batteries, and ensures that your alarm will go off on time even if you have a power outage while you’re sleeping.

The problem that I found is that the cord is so long it dangles down to far and is annoying to sleep with. If you zip it in the pouch it is hard to get back out.  Another problem is the volume most of the time is so soft I have to put the volume all the way up to be able to hear it.  Not sure if it is because the headphones speakers are not adjustable or if it is the head phones themselves.

I purchased four other Bluetooth speakers for my house over a several year period. I have a [[ASIN:B007ZG03DG Bose Wave Bluetooth Music Adapter]], which is not very good and a [[ASIN:B00MPMK3GW Goal Zero 94014 Rock Out 2 Green Solar Rechargeable Speaker]] which does not work when paired with some devices and, when it does pair well, it usually lacks the powerful sound I am looking for.

I also purchased one [[ASIN:B00SNBCBBY ION Audio Block Rocker (iPA76A) | Portable Bluetooth Speaker]] and one [[ASIN:B01N17AQ7U ION Audio IPA88 Tailgater Flash Wireless/Bluetooth Speaker]] both from Costco. I absolutely love the Block Rocker (except for when paired with my iPad Pro) and I only like the Tailgate Flash. The lights on the Tailgate Flash annoy me because they have to be turned off every time I power on the unit. Nevertheless, the sound from the ION speakers are usually awesome.

The IONs are the only ones I use frequently indoors (even though they are more of an outdoor Bluetooth speaker). They are powerful speakers and the sound is intense. However, I wanted something small and more portable and since the Goal Zero does not always function, I figured I would try this Sony.

What comes in the Sony box
- one Bluetooth speaker
- one micro USB charging cable
- one quick start guide
- one user guide - warns against using & leaving unit in a car or sauna but does not say much about how to operate this speaker
- one limited 1-year warranty insert
- one pamphlet about the SongPal app - a mobile app from Sony that allows the user to play music or audio from various devices and smartphones.

Features on the SONY

- It is rated as IPX5 water resistant (not waterproof but close enough; it probably will not soak through in a short burst of heavy rain). See link in comments section of review for description of ratings.

- It features a wireless party chain that allows a connection of up to 10 Bluetooth speakers at once. I did not try this feature. I am not sure if all in the party chain have to be Sony speakers or not.

- It has a speaker phone voice assist function to allow for hands free voice over IP through the speaker, which I was unable to get working.

- It lights up (great for party or listening to vibrant music). I love how the blue light pulsates to the music but it can be turned off if desired and once it is turned off, it remembers that setting until it is turned on again.

- It has a speaker add function for adding an extra Sony speaker for surround sound.

- It has up to 12 hours of battery life.

- It charges from most USB power sources including from the USB port on a laptop

These are the control buttons from left to right.

- Extra Bass Button (toggles on and off for extra bass); when held for a few seconds it turns off the blue perimeter light. I like that it remembers the last setting so if I turned off the light, the light will remain off until I choose to turn it on again.

- Phone Button for speaker phone assist; when held for a few seconds, it says the battery charge percentage. However, I found a quirk in the system. If I am charging the unit and turn it on to get the battery charge percentage, a woman’s voice came on and said 70%. However, if I unplugged the unit from a power source and turned it on, it said it was fully charged.

- Pause and Play toggle button

- Speaker Add button (Left/Right) for pairing another Sony speaker to this unit for surround sound.

- Minus button for lowering volume.

- Plus button for increasing volume.

- Power button for tuning the unit on. Once unit is powered on, hold the power button for a few seconds and then release it to pair a device to the Bluetooth speaker. Upon release, a female voice says “pairing” and then it beeps once it is paired.

I charged the speaker for a couple of hours before the first use but I am not sure it needed it as the battery indictor fluctuated between 100% and 70% charged depending on whether the unit was plugged in or not. The connector port is located behind the tiny cover on the back of the unit. I had trouble opening this with my fingernails.

I paired this speaker with the following devices.

- Google Nexus 7 Tablet (2013 version Android device) – the sound is moderately powerful.

- iPad Pro 12.9 – the sound is okay; I actually prefer the powerful sound that is supplied by the iPad Pro’s own speakers over this Sony speaker. The system wanted me to install SongPal as an option; I found it under another name and after installation, the app said it would probably slow down my iPad so I immediately deleted it.

- HP Omen Laptop – the sound is powerful and much better than the Omen’s own speakers.

- Dell Latitude E7470 Laptop – the sound is powerful and much better than the Dell’s own speakers.

As usual, I am disappointed in the user guide. It does not describe each button. It only mentions the Voice Guidance usage and does a poor job at that. However, the quick start guide pictorially shows the buttons as long as one can decipher the pictures.

In summary, the unit is sleek, simple, and shaped like a super-sized oblong pill. It is heavy at 1.45 pounds. When powered on, a blue perimeter light outlines the speaker and pulsates to music. I found this speaker to be moderately powerful when paired with three of the four devices I tried it on. I did not like the sound with the iPad Pro. To get the best performance, I needed to leave on the “Extra Bass.” The battery-charging indicator is a bit quirky and untrustworthy. The charge percentage was different depending on whether I was plugged in or not. I like that it is portable and water resistant. The instructions could be better and until I figured out the unit, I initially had trouble pairing. When using the phone button, I was unable to get voice over IP to route through the speaker no matter what I did. Overall, in comparison to my very portal Goal Zero speaker, this speaker is better. Although it is an unfair comparison, no portable speaker has yet to compare to my two ION speakers. I would have rated this four stars if it were not for the lousy written instructions, the quirky battery charge indicator, and its failure of the speaker phone voice assist. I was also very disappointed in the sound with my iPad Pro. Other than this, this speaker is a good contender for the right application.

I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

It seems to work fine for everything but games, and it seems that the sound processor may be the source of the audio and video glitches. Certain sounds seem to cause more problems than others, including dropped audio, glitchy video, and sometimes a blank screen. This happens with both XBox Ones and a PS3. I mainly play Forza 6 and Gran Turismo 6, and certain engine sounds seem to be associated with these problems more than others. Streaming video doesn't seem to cause any problems with any of the input devices or either TV. The normal solution is to cycle the power off and back on. Different cables or settings don't seem to make a difference. I'm not using the audio splitter at all. Personal opinion (from decades of experience with processors of all kinds), is that whatever processor is used simply cannot process some sounds correctly, even to pass the signal through. I may be wrong. I've been wrong before. This may be a quality control issue, or it may be an engineering issue. Either way, I'm looking for a better product, and most of the ones in this price range seem to be identical except for the name on the box. In fact, many more expensive devices seem to be exactly the same layout, and likely use the same circuitry. There's no way to tell from the name on the box, or the Amazon description.

I wanted to find a cheaper alternative to my wife's wireless Bose headset, something with decent noise cancelling for flights and work. So far I've used Bose, the MPOW H5, Treblab, and Woltix with ANC.

The sound on these are first class - really great highs, mids, and lows - tons of clarity (when active noise cancel is on...otherwise it sounds a bit muggy). Very comfortable and light. BUT - I got these because they are wireless with active noise cancellation, and although the ANC is effective, if you are in a quiet room you'll hear a slight hiss when the ANC is on - many people report the same thing in reviews, and it's true - you'll hear it. You won't notice this when music is on or during a flight. I often use these at coffee shops just to zone out and focus on work, and I could notice the slight hiss in quieter environments.

I've also used Bose, the MPOW H5, and Woltix with ANC. I didn't want to buy another Bose headset when my wife and I travel together. Nothing will compare to Bose noise cancellation, but the MPOW H5 and Woltix are actually really nice for the money. The MPOW H5 don't have as good audio clarity as the Treblab, but at the end of the day I got noise cancelling headphones for the noise canceling. I ended up returning the Treblab and the MPOW H5 and I kept the Woltix because they are more comfortable than the MPOW and had the best low-price ANC. The MPOW also had some sound interference issues randomly when the ANC was on.

So:

Bose: Best noise cancellation, good audio, comfortable, but definitely expensive!
Treblab: Best audio, worst noise cancellation (you can hear a slight hiss when turned on), comfortable, but large and they don't fold down too small.
MPOW: Good audio, good noise cancellation, but was getting some weird sound interference with the ANC on sometimes. Tight on ears.
Woltix: Good audio, good noise cancellation, most comfortable (way lighter and less tight on the ears than the MPOW), and fold down the smallest.

When reviewing headsets, I don't just pop them on and hit play on a favorite song or take a call. I actually run them through a battery of sound tests from an audio site. I run all sets through the same test to make it fair. First on my PC and then on my iPhone XS. I find it's the best way to make an unbiased review.
• Bass: Poor with a limited range. It also wasn’t balanced between the earbuds.
• High freq: Better than the bass, but still a limited range. It was balanced between the earbuds much better though.
• Rattle: None, but it would be weird if earbuds rattled. Ok that’s not true, I stepped on a pair at the gym that rattled afterwards. Oops.
• Volume: Sufficient. I don’t blast my earbuds, because I like to keep my hearing. I could turn it low enough to not hear, and loud enough to be uncomfortable.
• Clarity: Isolated for the sound test they did fine. However, outside the site the clarity started to degrade, and on a call was bad enough to be an issue.

The sound check results were mediocre. Bass was lacking, as was the general range of the set. These actually did worse than their cheaper behind the neck set (Jabra Evolve 65e UC).

As for things other than sound, like usability I like to ask myself what I’m looking for and if product meets those expectations. So, here goes:

Would these last the entire workday?
Yes and No, if you take them off to charge during lunch then you will probably be fine. Otherwise no they are going to die out about 75% through a standard 8 hr workday. They require a USB port and their little case thing to charge. I had no issues as long as I remember to charge them at lunch.

Are they easy to use?
The basics, yes. All the extra features, not so much. I opened the box up and was happy to see the quick-start guide, unfortunately if there is a manual I didn't get one. I found a digital copy tucked away in the iPhone app, but nothing in the box itself. That made anything past the basics in the quick-start guide a matter of trial and error, until I found the manual tucked away in the App. For the price, that seems like a rather cheap move. There is a ton of useful info in the manual that is not contained in the quick-start guide.

Can I take calls seamlessly?
Yes, but for me at least the call experience was lacking. The voices on some but not all calls were a bit muddled, however they could hear me just fine. So poor marks for the sound quality, but high marks for the mic.
Speaking of mics, can I mute the mic easily?
Easily, yes. But knowing for sure if you are muted (we've all been there) only when using the computer dongle, on my iPhone using Bluetooth, eek not so much. Had to leave it to faith. That was a bit scary.

Plays music well (aka does it have range and bass)?
Meh. I have the sound review at the top. As you can imagine, lack of bass negatively impacts listening to music. I mean it wasn’t awful but it wasn’t great either.

Can I opt to hear people talking to me (audio pass-through)?
Yes, but it sounds super static and buzzy. The sound is not clear and crisp at all. Also, you can't just pop an earbud out and listen with one ear. If the earbuds are anymore than head-width apart they stop working all together. According to the manual, you should be able to use the right earbud by itself, but that was not my experience. It also would stop working (although it worked a bit longer than the left) once they were too far apart.

Noise-canceling abilities, can I at least block out the cubical next to me?
Sort of. You can block drumming blah blah blah sounds, but ringing phones and coworkers talking, not so much. Although it did take the edge off. The Jabra iPhone app for these has some cool ambient sound machine settings, waves crashing, thunderstorm, white noise, etc. Probably my favorite thing about this whole set.

Are they comfortable?
I didn't like them, but I am a petite human and have small ears. I also don't like the weird vacuuming pressure you feel when wearing anything noise-cancelling. I will give these neutral marks for comfort, I think if you had larger ear canals and didn't mind closed type headsets these would probably be fine.

Are these worth the price?
Nope. For the price these should be spectacular and check all the boxes. They are mediocre in sound quality even though they are packed with features. If you plan on just tossing them on and not actually testing the audio, go for it. They work. But for the price, they should handle music and calls equally well. They do not.

Overall, I will have to say I was rather disappointed with these. I also reviewed their behind the neck version (Jabra Evolve 65e UC) and was hoping I had just gotten a dud with that set. Well lightening either struck twice, or the audio on these is even worse than the cheaper behind the neck version. Darn, because I wanted to love these. I have a soft spot for gadgets with cool features. These had potential. I will give them three stars because if the price point wasn’t so high, they would be okay. Not great, but they’d get the job done. I also really liked the ambient sounds you could listen to on the app. A nice little extra that was unexpected.

Hope that helps!

That aside, the sound quality was ok, with a somewhat tinny, canned quality and poor capability in processing deep bass or treble. If changing the levels to decrease treble, you'll see some improvement in the sound. For anything spoken word like podcasts, these are fine.
The fit is not bad. Usually, these things are big on me (female with apparently small ear-holes, if you would judge by most headphones), but these were comfortable. The three sizes of rubbery earplugs always help and are generally standard, and the ear hooks also aide in keeping them in place.

Summary:
For the price, you get decent headphones that do not have an output function.

While the pairing process was simple, and the ability to make calls went smoothly, the sound quality was sub-par. One might expect this level of quality in a $10 headphone.
Here's why:
-The volume tops out at somewhere in the 80 decibel range, which is not a lot. It would be fine for background listening in a quiet environment, but if you want to listen to music loudly, which many people might, or if you are dealing with lots of background noise, then it's not even remotely adequate.
-Does nothing for treble or bass. Everything sounds right around the middle, flattening out most music.
-Lacks detail. You don't hear the quieter elements in music, and it does not pick up on individual parts. Fuzzy.

I wouldn't buy these. Bluetooth headsets can be very hit or miss. While it was user-friendly, this was mostly a miss.

The portability is excellent, as well as a few other features: it is rechargeable, very small, lightweight, and the pairing process is so easy. Unfortunately, this product has several downsides, and they are the ones that count most: the sound quality is bad.

I always wonder why products allow you to raise the volume far beyond the limits of what the product can sustain without creating distortion. The point at which the product does this is roughly halfway; it can only go to roughly 65-80 decibels before treble starts to sound horrible, distorted, and messy. That is NOT very loud at all. The sound, even at lower volumes, is somewhat fuzzy: you cannot hear detail in the music like you can with better quality speakers. Even With the distortion, at maximum volume, it doesn't get Very loud. That's mostly to be expected at this price point and in something of this size with rechargeable batteries, you can't hope for much more than this product has to offer. For that reason, it gets 3 stars. Roughly average--not great, not terrible.

This is the second "Creative" brand wireless bluetooth speaker with microphone, and so far, the sound quality has not been very good. The first, "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone" was $127.04 (list price $149.99), and this one currently has a list price of $199.99. I cannot hear any discernable difference in sound quality, though this speaker is larger than the other. They are both OK for being usb powered, but there are better-sounding products out there for the same price if you are willing to sacrifice the speaker option.

I ran the same tests on this speaker as the other and got identical results:

This one gets a mixed review for the overall sound quality, but it does have some features that make it very useful. I will be reviewing its various features individually so you can better assess if this meets your needs or not. I used a decibel measuring app on my phone to determine when the speakers began to distort some of what I played.

Playing audio with Bluetooth or via USB with a computer:
-There is no noticeable difference with playback using Bluetooth versus USB connection to a computer, and it has a Very long range (I walked about 25ft away and it was still doing fine)

AUDIO

75 DECIBELS AND UNDER:
Almost all audio was fine: clear, undistorted, and with pretty good clarity (don't expect GREAT quality or clarity. Just Good.) Some types of music fared poorly even at this relatively soft volume. I used "Fortuna from Carmina Burana" to test the system's limits. (YouTube the piece if you want to know which song I refer to--you'll recognize it immediately) The chorus of singers sounded distorted. At higher volumes, even as lot as 85db, it was awful. Other types of music were fine (orchestra music, pop, hip hop, electronica), but sometimes the treble was a bit fuzzy.

75-85 DECIBELS:
This is the maximum volume the speakers can reach with the USB connection, so it can get loud enough for a small-medium party, but not Very loud.
It's hit and miss here. The treble and bass have some problems, especially treble. The clarity diminishes and any nuances in your music will generally get a bit lost or muffled. Choral music, music with higher pitched percussive elements, and some types of rock and orchestra music don't sound very good.

PHONE CALLS:
The voice of the person you are calling sounds a bit muffled--definitely not as good as headphones or the phone, but about on par with other Bluetooth systems I've tried.

The voice of the speaker (i.e. You) is actually clear! This part gets a solid review. With my built-in car Bluetooth system, as well as detachable ones I've reviewed, usually the person you are calling has trouble hearing you and can experience interference. Maybe that is because it is in the car and there's road noise, but in any case, the fact this one does, actually, sound clear to the recipient of your phone call is a BIG plus.

Overall, this is a good product when you compare it to other desktop laptop speakers. If you are comparing it to products specifically meant for enjoying audio, however, I would recommend the Pioneer Electronics Audition Series for a relatively inexpensive but high quality experience, or Bose if you are looking for something higher-end. The price of the Pioneer product is almost the same, and while it doesn't have Bluetooth unless you buy the attachment separately (about $70) and it only docks with the older iPhone and iPods, the sound quality of that one is stunning. If you want extra features like FREE Bluetooth and speakerphone capability, this one is ok for the price. Not great. Just ok.

Because this is basically the same as the "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone", and the other is about $70 cheaper, I would recommend getting the SBX10 and saving your money. They are basically the same thing, so either pay more and get better sound quality with another product entirely, or pay less for the same thing.

This is a decent speaker with some nice touches, but only for those who listen to music occasionally and are fine with "good enough if I can hear it" sound. Details

Size: relative small footprint--bigger than a lot of better sounding bluetooth speakers, but also comes with extras so can't fault them on size.

Pairing: paired easily and immediately with all our IOS devices--phones and iPads, and our Mac laptops. Never lost signal

Clock: nice and bright, easy to read, easy to set

Q1 charge-worked with all our compatible devices with no problems at all, couldn't be easier to use

battery life about as promised--we went 6+ hours twice

dual speakers are distinguishable

The downside as noted at the top is sound. It isn't horrible--it's clear enough. But it's definitely thin if not tinny, and lacks a full, rich output/range. We have a Denon, a Jam, and a UE Boom, and all are noticeably, significantly better, richer, fuller sounding. (they obviously don't come with clocks or wireless charging).

that said, my wife thought his sounded "fine". It's all in your expectations and desires. I would not use this as a listening device; she'd be perfectly happy with it. So know where you are in the "how good does my music need to be and how often do I listen to it" spectrum

Short story of the review is that these are just as they say they are--a pair of relatively inexpensive "basic" earphones. As such, they seem to be a decent value and have some good points, but if you're looking for sound quality over price, you'll want to go elsewhere.

Pros:
Packaging: small and minimalist as it should be

Provided with: multiple size earbuds caps and ear inserts (more on these later), a very short charging cable, and a decent zip-around traveling pouch

Pairing: No problem with any of my Apple devices. Instantly recognized and paired with an iPhone (8 and 6), iPad (Pro and Air 2), and MacBook Pro. Couldn't be quicker or easier each and every time

Comfort: This was an issue for me, though obviously this is a pretty subjective category. I had to step down immediately to the small caps/rings, which is no surprise--I do that with I think all of my earbuds. But even with the smalls I just couldn't get a a good seal or a comfortable, though oddly enough much worse with my right. The left was not "great" but was certainly good; right was a bad seal and wholly uncomfortable no matter what I tried. Weird.

Sound quality: Again, it's a matter of pricing here. I don't own many basics and it's been years since I've had a set of lower-tier earbuds, so it's hard for me to compare at an equal level. The sound is what I'd call adequate, especially for exercise or listening to an audiobook. But there's no comparison to my PowerBeats3 or Jaybird X2s, and not even to my Jabra Elites, which I"d call my mid-range ones. The first two are in a whole other class in terms of range, sharpness, richness, and comfort, while the Jabras are a good step up in both sound and comfort. Sound here is more than a little thin at both ends, and just not very rich or full. Less noticeable with an audiobook, but definitely not the buds I'd choose if I'm focusing on listening to music, as opposed to having background sound while I"m doing something else. Phone quality is pretty similar--adequate, at times a bit muddy.

Controls: easy, intuitive, and responsive

Overall, if you want a basic set where quality of sound isn't a deal breaker, or a pair of cheaper ones for places you might have to worry about forgetting them, these will suit the bill, assuming you don't have the same comfort issue I did. But for someone looking for rich, full sound, particularly for music, I'd strongly advise moving up the ladder

I found it odd, reading some of these reviews, which claimed that these Sonys were definitely better than the Pioneer BS22s. Very odd indeed. It makes me wonder if they either weren't directly comparing the two back and forth, or didn't have the Pioneers set up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off.

To my ears, the Sonys aren't much better than the Micca MB42x. They both have slightly elevated treble, and are rather thin and one-note sounding in their presentation. Not a lot of depth or punch.

The BS22s however, you really "feel" the music. The soundstage is very open, and everything sounds larger even though the woofers are only 4" compared to the 5-1/4" SSCS5s. There is depth and a musicality that just can't be matched by the Sonys, and it's apparent right away. It's like they almost disappear and you're just left with the music. Most speakers in this price range are going to sound similar to the SSCS5/MB42x, not many if any are going to sound like the Pioneers.

I must have switched back and forth 200-300 times comparing the two, trying to convince myself that the Sonys were better than they were. I got them at $73 and the BS22s at $99, so I really wanted to like the SSCS5s.

It was always obvious which speaker was superior though - not once did I say "oh, the Sonys really sound better here". That's not to say these are bad speakers, but I don't think they're worth much more than $73, the sale price. The Pioneers however I'd be willing to pay their retail price and a bit more. If you're really on a budget, you could be satisfied with these ~$73, especially if you're only concerned about watching movies. But if you are willing to pay $20 more for the Pioneers when they're on sale (or even at $129), I'd recommend it.

Just remember to set the BS22s up properly: ~6 feet apart, toed in toward the listener, ear level, grills off. Also make sure they're properly amped.

The SSCS5s are decent and cheap enough that I decided to use my old receiver with them at my computer. I'd probably prefer them over the MB42X slightly, but that's about it.

With a budget sub like the Dayton SUB-1200 properly placed (subwoofer crawl) along with the BS22s, you'll have a system that sounds very nice and hits above its weight class - trust me on that. It used to be that headphones were a cheaper investment than speakers and you could get a better sound for less, but this set up edges out my HE-500/Bifrost/Asgard 2 and it's actually cheaper. Didn't think that was possible.

I've had these earbuds for a few months now and thought I'd revise my review.

My main gripe with these expensive but ultimately underwhelming earbuds is that they make a "thwomping" sound inside your ear drum whenever you jog or walk fast with them. I was at the gym recently and the sound of the earbuds jostling about in my ears was distracting. I don't recall ever having that problem with cheaper earbuds. This sound persisted even after I customized the buds to fit the shape of my ear.

On the positive side, the sound is decent though the bass and treble weren't that impressive. Its most effective feature was the noise-cancelling feature, which effectively blocked out any other noise. It worked so well that I would never use these buds while driving, crossing traffic or walking alone home late at night. With the spate of iPhone robberies, it's better to be able to hear a stranger's footsteps behind you. It's perfect, however, when you're on a subway or a bus and you want to block out that annoying person next to you who insists on complaining about her day.

The set includes a microphone for your iphone, which I don't use that much but works well enough - I heard my friend's voice on the other end of the line in very crisp, clear tones.

What's convenient is that the buds work with even the oldest ipods around. From the classic 2009 model to the most up to date Nano. Sony was smart to do this - that means a lot of people, not just techies with the most up-to-date devices, can use this. As an example, a friend of mine still has a working iPod mini (don't laugh, he's a Luddite!) and we tested the headset on that too. Surprisingly, it worked! - though the volume controls did not work with such an old, outdated model.

Another convenience is the location of the controls, which are located on a box located on the cord, which prevents you from having to reach all the way down to your iPod or iPhone to adjust the volume. My second favorite feature is the included clip, which allows me to wind up any slack on the cord and prevent it from getting tangled easily. In the past, I've killed so many earbuds because I pulled too hard on the cord by accident, so this is a welcome feature.

This deluxe model includes a pouch that offers an array of different sized earbuds - one set is noise-cancelling, while the other isn't. This is overkill, though. I tried out different sets of buds but none of them fit just right. And the "thwoping" sound I mentioned earlier still remained.

So I have mixed feelings about this product. The "thwomping" (sucking) sound is its biggest drawback for me, as the buds work best when you don't move around a lot.

Issue may be subjective, nevertheless... the issue is a quite flat sound, in particular the bass. The non-audiophile (i.e. reasonably priced) receivers used to have a "contour", or "bass boost" function (even the previous Sony model had it), which greatly enhanced the audibility of lower frequencies when played at low decibels. This one lacks it (and it sounds like most of nowadays sold receivers are like this), hence the sound coming out is quite flat (also for treble band), unless you go really loud. In addition, the receiver lacks a sub-woofer output, so there is no chance to improve low frequencies.
Out of the other available receivers, I decided to pick (by recommendation) a little more up-scale (yet still reasonably priced) Harman Kardon HK 3390 (2 x 80W) Stereo Receiver, which has sub-woofer outputs - even though it also lacks bass boost, I am expecting it will revive the bass, even with my old Sony 10" sub.

Power isn't everything. My intention was for the A90 to replace an old portable DAC/Amp combo that is only rated at 1.6W total at 75Ω. Sadly, the A90 made everything sound a bit thin and lifeless. It's like it has the negative characteristics of an overly clinical sounding amp without any of the positives like extracting detail.

It's not a horrible amp. It's just not a great amp. Maybe the A90 would sound better when paired with muffled/veiled or extremely warm sounding headphones. For Sennheiser HD800's or HD820's though, which are inherently bright, it's a horrible match. The A90 sucked the soul from the music with those particular headphones.

The chain I tested with the A90 was a Naim ND5 XS2 streamer > Nordost Silver Shadow BNC > Schiit Gungnir Multibit DAC > Cardas Clear XLR > Topping A90. There's usually a Schiit Mjolnir 2 at the end of the chain and it sounds amazing. I didn't expect the A90 to outperform the Mjolnir but I did expect it to outperform my little DAC/Amp combo, especially when being fed such a good source

All I can really take away from my experience with the A90 is DO NOT pair this amp with bright headphones. Can't comment on other headphones but avoid this amp if you've got HD800's or 820's.

The Onkyo HT-S5100 Home Entertainment System sounded quite good when listening to the radio, and I really loved the self-calibration feature to set the speaker phase/power-level based upon our optimum seating position.

When the receiver is played at low to mid volume ranges, the system was impressive, but there was distoration at higher levels when the speakers were driven beyond their capabilities.

As far as a Stereo Receiver goes, I'd give it high marks, but as far as a Home Entertainment system goes... in my opinion, I'd purchase something else.

I found after many frustrating hours of trying to get the receiver to work with my other HDMI components, that all of my attempts were in vain.

I'd essentially purchased the system on the recommedation of Consumer Reports (They crowed about the HT-S5100 having the best sound of any system they'd ever tested, and it was one of the only ones offering 7.1 versus 5.1 stereo surround).

I eventually re-read the Onkyo Owners Manual and found a small blurb regarding the audio of the system not working with HDMI...

I freely admit I'd blown-off the fact that analog/digital connectors were shown on the Quick Hook-Up illustrations (thinking these were alternative connections for those unlucky soul's who didn't have HDMI), when I finally resorted to contacting Onkyo for assistance/confirmation.

They confirmed my worst-fear, their HDMI's were (Pass-Though). When asked why they even bothered to put HDMI connectors on the system, the reply was (some consumers desired them).

Personally, I feel if a system has HDMI connectors present, that is implies they're fully compliant, otherwise their presence is misleading.

What this meant was all of my new toy's (50" Plasma, Blu-ray player, and Xbox 360) could only pass on video (not the higher quality audio signals through the HDMI connectors), and that I'd have to accept a lower quality audio output due to the use of standard audio connectors.

Perhaps I'd missed this in CR's review (or it wasn't stated), as I had to purchase additional digital cabling so that I could even hear the audio content of the devices hooked into the Onkyo (added expense/wiring woe's).

If I had to do it all over again, I'd purchase the HT-S5100 as a Stereo Receiver, but I wouldn't recommend it as the hub for a Home Entertainment System to interconnect your HDMI devices.

I shoved all but about a foot of the cable back behind the stereo and it passes smoothly through the hole as needed but my phone rarely leaves the Spigen magentic vent phone holder in my car.

10/15/18: docked 2 stars- cable stopped working- threw off horrid feedback and couldn't stand using to listen to my phone in my car after barely 6 months. It was never kinked, damaged, or abused, it was kept tied in loose loop and simply plugged into and removed from my phone 1-3 x a day. No reason for it to stop working. Trying an Anker brand cable and if it can't last at least a year I'm done with aux cables, I'll upgrade to Grom bluetooth.

I have tried a few "bone conduction" headphones. The way you can tell if they are bone conduction is because you can still hear the sound with earplugs in. These are true bone conduction, but the volume is much quieter than others at this price point.

The first 2 of these (for different Galaxy S20+ phones) worked flawlessly for about a year. Then mine became intermittent in working, and being it lasted a year, I felt I'd gotten my money's worth and purchased another in red. That one only lasted about 4 months. So, I purchased another one in grey, but it arrived defective (it was slid out of its casing) so I returned and purchased another one. This latest one (also in grey) works, but it has a loud snap sound whenever I either plug it in, or sometimes just start a new app. I'm so tired of returning these (and an unfortunate series of other items that were defective), so I just kept it. I sure hope Samsung will return the headphone jack to their phones, or my next phone won't be a Samsung. Being that I'm disabled and in bed 22 hours a day, wireless headphones aren't be a good option for me, as I'd constantly run them out of charge.

When this adapter works, it works well, but they seem to have more of a short term lifespan.
The sound is "ok", but the quality is very low. I've owned much better headphones for the same price.

I realized after wearing these for about an hour why they must have been on sale on Amazon. The cord from the headphones to the media device comes right out the bottom in a non-flexible way. Therefore it bumps my shoulders and introduces a weird static type sound to the music playing. They're okay now that I know to hold my shoulder a certain way and what the noise is if I lose the position but I wouldn't buy them again.

Update. 11/27/2020 Only A little over a year old and only used the on nightstand. The cord cover split. Given the price of this thing, I’m surprised. Very poor quality materials.

The earphones work great while the phone also charges. However, there is a big negative in that if the phone wiggles, the phone makes bing noises, like that bing it makes when the charger is first attached. This is a drag at night because others hear it. On the previous iPhones, 4 and 5S, if the headphone was in the headphone jack, any sound from attaching the charger was silenced. With this adapter, it’s not silenced. Again, if attached, the bing sound occurs every time the phone wiggles. Troublesome during the night.

I used this amplifier to boost the sound coming out of a Sennheiser headset while doing training through the internet. Since this is my occupation, and I have hearing loss and wear hearing aides, the use of the headset without the amp did not produce loud enough sound for comfortable conversation. This little amp boosted the sound perfectly, the size allowed me to carry it for use in different locations, and I was a happy camper. I just found, after four months, that I lost sound in one side of the headset, and by inserting and removing the amp and changing connections discovered that the problem is in the amp, not the headset or computer. Not sure if I should get another one of these or something else, loved the portability of it. Will have to look into the warranty, sure I no longer have the paperwork.
Update 5/2016: Amazon did begrudgingly refund the price of this amp (a Warehouse purchase, so they balked at warranty) and I purchased another, only to have it also die in a few months like the first. Will try to exercise the warranty on this one, but basically have a extra on hand or get another device...just not a lot this small. Looking for recommendations on something else.

I love this camera, but I use it mainly for the microphone. It works very well for both video and sound. However, there is no way to put the microphone volume on 0, which still picks up sound, and make 0 the default volume. Every time I restart the pc, the microphone volume goes back up to the same level as the system volume.... and it squeals and shreeks  so loud until I am able to pull up the system volume and put it back to 0. With sensitive ears, and restarting my pc a few times per week, this is ridiculous for such a nice web cam, and it seems there should be a fix for it.

I'm mainly using this for language-learning CDs, and am grateful to have something this compact and easy for playback; however, trying it with music the sound is atrocious. There are a few EQ settings all bad (jazz the least bad, at least there's some treble and it's not totally muddy). The top third of volume (20-30) is distorted listening to music both CD and Spotify using the Bluetooth. I got a fanny pack with a Bluetooth speaker that I listened to right after this for the first time and it blew this away.

If you're looking for something to watch a movie on or videos, this isn't too bad for the money but if you're looking for great sound and TV quality, this isn't the tablet you want. I so wanted to love this because I need a tablet but the response time while browsing and the overall quality is very poor but for the price it would be decent for movies and maybe some games. The Speakers are on the back which isn't the best idea when you can't hear them good. If they would put the speakers on the front then it would improve movie watching immensely. The camera is kid quality at best. It definitely doesn't take  print worthy photos; the focus is blurred and not sharp at all. I only gave it 3 stars because for the money, it's probably decent.

Well, I wanted to love this little speaker but the sound isn't very good. Now, with that said, it's advertised that you can use it with a TV but I definitely wouldn't recommend it, the sound isn't good enough for that but when it's hooked to a phone for music, it's not too bad. If you want a little sound amplification for a phone call or some non-blaring music, it would work for that. It's fairly easy to operate and pair with another device.

These are OK, but not as good as the ones that came with my iPhone. Also, they say they work with an iPhone, but they don’t work with my iPhone 7 that has a lightning adapter and not one of these 3.5 mm ones.
The sound quality was not as bright as the ones that came with my iPhone. As a matter of fact, they didn’t deliver the volume that the iPhone earbuds did. I’m giving them three stars because they were very comfortable.

Although there are a lot of positive points to be said about this product, a major flaw with it is that - even on low volumes and on songs without much bass - you can hear a bit of distortion, like crackly static, that sounds like a speaker that you're either working too hard or is at the end of its life. This becomes worse as the battery gets low. I consider this issue to be "understandable and sort of acceptable" considering the whole system has to run on battery power and most people aren't expecting high power out of such a setup. They might just have a high-pass crossover set too high to conserve power, and too much is cut off, resulting in messy sound.

When you charge your phone with the speaker's battery (which in itself is sort of a nice, if cannibalistic, feature, one that other devices claim even though it is inherent to the device; with this, the USB-A port was added specifically for this purpose), it lowers the volume to level 8 (there is nothing to tell you what level you're at) to keep from draining the battery quickly. Even at this medium level and below, this problem can be recognized.

The bike mounts are 4" apart, center to center, so make sure you have room on your bike handlebars if that is your purpose for ordering. Included bike mounts are good. It also comes with a neoprene case, a USB cable, and an audio cable, both red. With all these extras trying to give the appearance of premium, it doesn't actually come with a charger, not that this will be an issue for most people (you probably already have more than you know what to do with).

There should be keyhole slots built into the bike mounts so it could also be hung on the wall and removed easily, making it more versatile.

The unit pairs easily and immediately with my Blackberry every time, and it can control the tracks through the BT connection as well. It looks well made and has a good feel to it. It looks like it could almost be waterproof, although I noticed no mention or claim of that feature (so I'm sure it's not).

The sound overall isn't bad for a low voltage battery operated speaker, as long as you're not sitting down and listening too closely. I guess for the purposes of making noise as you ride around the neighborhood, it'll do just fine.
The Volume on this is not loud at all. IT is nice and convenient to keep on your belt but I wish it had more volume.

The sound quality is pretty poor - on my Samsung Note, I have to go to max volume to be able to hear anything clearly (when experimenting with both buds, it seems to be slightly better).  The touch controls are very finicky and not very intuitive.  It does block noise well, but that doesnt translate to better audio quality for listening to music (primary use was for walking/jogging).  They fit fine and didnt have any issues when doing yard work or jogging.  The unit seems to keep the charge as advertised.  But the biggest issue is of course is the sound volume and quality - even at this pricepoint - this is not a good value.  For a backup or travel purposes where you wont beat yourself up if you misplace or lose , there are better options available.

These earbuds are not especially impressive. I would have given them 3.5 stars if I could have. The noise cancelation is pretty decent. The earbuds last the five hours they say they do. The earbuds don't get very loud, which would perhaps be good for a child or teenager to protect their hearing. For an adult, though, it can be a bit frustrating in situations where you really want to rock out. The charging case is adequate. In all, it covers all its claims, but there just isn't anything impressive about the sound quality and shorter battery life.

This is an interesting device as a scientific experiment, but not a very good quality speaker. It is interesting as a novelty, but if you care about the quality of sound in your music, I would not recommend it.

Overall, these are a generally OK pair of headphones. While the sound quality won't please an audiophile, it is more than acceptable for general use. I found them to be better suited for movie watching rather than music listening since the bass and upper range are rather muted. Decent quality midrange.

It scores pretty high with regard to comfort. Lightweight, easy to adjust, and nicely cushioned.

I was not impressed with the noise cancellation feature. Yes, it does cut down on some background noise when the cancellation feature is engaged (simple switch on the earpiece turns it on and off; it runs on a AAA battery). But, the sound isolation is actually less than I get with a quality pair of properly-fitted ear buds. I could easily hear ambient sounds with the headphones on.

The track skipping feature does not work with the Fire. The manufacturer does not claim it would, so no stars are detracted for that. I mention it only in case Fire owners are thinking about using that feature. Other than that, it works perfectly with the Fire - made it much more enjoyable to watch videos than using the internal speakers.

I'll give this 3 stars. It offers OK sound quality and decent comfort, but it's billed as having noise cancellation, and that feature is not well implemented.

I definitely prefer to use Bluetooth earbuds any day over wired, but sometimes it can't be helped.  Such as times when my Bluetooth earbuds weren't charged.  The sound of these is o.k. but not what you'd be getting from a high end pair.  I teach classical guitar so my acid test for any earbud is playing that and seeing how it sounds.  I'm doing it now and the trebles come through o.k. but the bass is pretty weak.  These will be good to keep a pair in my car or purse for those times when my Bluetooths won't work for whatever reasons.  The volume doesn't work so it has to be adjusted on the device they're plugged into.  They come with extra earbud covers and they feel fine in my female ears the way they are.  I don't know what these cost as of this review but I wouldn't want to pay more than $15.00 for them.

The earbuds I received for review don't have external volume control.  I have to adjust the volume using my phone or whatever device I have these plugged into.  I had my husband call me and the call button on the earbud cord worked fine. These are fine for in the car and yakking on the phone but if you want to listen to music it would be best to get a much better set of earbuds.  These don't have any bass to speak of, and the sound is thin and tinny.  You get a couple more pairs of bud covers for a better fit.  No instructions come with these but it's not really necessary since they're easy to figure out.

This is a great idea and I see that it works really well in other people's cars, but I just can't get it loud enough.  I don't want it ear drum breaking or anything near that, I don't like it super loud anyway, but when driving the road noise nearly drowns it out even when it's at full volume and my speakers are turned full up on.  Besides that, I had trouble finding a blank station and only found one, but when I connected the device and my car radio to it I got too much static.  So, I tried using the auxiliary cable since the instructions said if you can't find a blank station then use the aux.  I have a 1996 Honda  Civic and it has an auxiliary port so I connected the Guanda transmitter to my radio through it and Bluetooth to my phone.  The static was gone, but the volume was still a problem.  I like that I can use a micro card that has the music I want on it, but it will always have the volume problem.  The device looks very nice and is basically intuitive.

I can't get this system loud enough to please me. I often like my music loud and raucousy! It says 40 watts but if you want some volume to fill up your room I don't think you'll be happy with this system. Right now I'm listening to, "Boogaloo Chevere" (tropical) and I have it cranked up to full volume and it's just not coming through like I expected. I have the sub-woofer bass turned full volume but I hear little bass and the horns and voices sound squeezed and strained. I'm thinking that the cheesy-thin auxiliary 3.5 mm input cable that comes with this system might be the reason. It's very thin and weak. Definitely needs to be more robust. Granted, I'm listening to music on my PC downloaded from I-tunes, but I think the set of 25 watt Logitech speakers (Logitech Z313 Speaker System) I had on before sounded better and at 1/3 the price of these. Where's my 40 watts of power here?!

I have this system set up straight from the box using what was included. The speakers are supposedly wall-mountable but no hardware was included so they're sitting on my desk, one on each side of monitor. The sub-woofer tower is underneath my desk and even with the bass turned up full I can only detect minimal bass output from it aurally and when I put my hand over the top of it I can barely feel any vibrations coming from it. I'm really kind of disappointed......why did they include such a cheap audio cable???

The satellite speakers look basically like a pair of binoculars turned up on their side. They look alright and are steady enough on their stands. I don't think I would mount these things on the wall anyway. I haven't tried connecting 3 different inputs yet, just my PC, but you can hook up to 3 external devices. The control knob is easy to use. You have to turn the big black knob to control the volume and to turn it completely off. The sub-woofer control knob is also on the main control knob. I have my control knob lying on floor beside my CPU. I have to reach down and pick it up to use it or else deal with having more cables on my desk.

My biggest disappointment is the way the classical guitar comes across on this system. I have to have the volume turned on nearly full blast to try to hear all the tones and colors of the instrument. My own home classical guitar recordings come across very weak and muted out as compared to the sounds on the Z313 system. Believe me, I am not hard of hearing and can hear a fly pooter, so I know what sounds clear and loud and what does not. But again, I think it's due to the cheap cable. I'm going to find a much better cable, try it out and report back. So for now, the 3 star stays.

UPDATE 9.28.12
I bought a Monster cable for twenty dollars and it only helps improve the sound minimally. I'm really surprised that this is the most volume I can get for 40 watts. It still gets loud for most types of music, but the classical guitar just doesn't carry as well on these speakers as it does on the cheaper set of speakers I had before.

The headphones are designed well and comfortable, but the bass delivered was somewhat disappointing. The noise cancellation and battery life were great though. I see that these have since been discounted and at the current price point they are a much better buy.

I don't really like in-ear buds and use around ear headphones at home. This seemed like a decent on the go solution, but they seem like more trouble than they're worth. I haven't had issues with disconnecting or not having native English voice prompts, but they just don't seem to "do it" for me.

By nature of the fact they fit on the outside of the ear, they're not the loudest even at max volume. The design is nice because it allows me to hear people talking without having to pause the music or remove the headphones, but I wouldn't consider these as possessing any noise canceling properties.

They don't fit snug either and if I manage to get them into a position where they don't move around a bit, they'll begin causing discomfort after a brief period. I feel like I'm constantly adjusting them, which leads to me triggering the very sensitive touch function. I'm not positive how the touch functionality works, as it sometimes pauses the music as expected but often randomly controls volume.

They work and everybody's different, but they're ultimately too touchy, don't fit well and aren't loud enough.

Overall the sound quality isn't poor but placement is going to play a bigger role in quality achieved. The remote feels cheap and flimsy, but is the only way to alter advanced sound options. It's a fairly average product and it seems for everything to like here is something that disappoints. Most of all, I have issues with the sound dropping for periods. I've tried multiple sources and all three input methods and it still seems the sound cuts out at random times before coming back. A middling product that I can't fully recommend but also wouldn't consider trash bin material.

Overall, the product works. You're going to get audio that's a bit better than the cheap speakers on your computer monitor, certainly louder audio, but not necessarily the most crisp audio. They're tuned toward the low end and the audio feels like it has good body but seems muddy on the high end. Ultimately better than nothing but not amazing. You can shut off the RGB lights, which I was worried you may not.

Better than nothing but certainly not better than their price.
This is just ok. I was disappointed in this item.  The sound is not crisp, and I would not try others.. waste of money.

The bass is really underwhelming and at first I thought the subwoofer was broke. I might actually just return it and get something that actually thumps the beats like the soundbar I have for the tv.  Too bad they made it basically kid friendly governed so you cant turn up the bass individually.  Its too loud for the neighbors before you can even start to tell there's even a subwoofer hooked up.
Overall it is okay, I really like the color purple. The volume quality is not that good. It is used when you workout, but the length of earbuds is a little bit long.

I want to return it .

I have a 3-year old Bose Cinemate that is 3 times smaller AND SOUNDS waaaaay better.
